--- title: "Tutorial 1 · The pipeline: split, recipe, workflow, baseline" subtitle: "Session 2 · Day 1, 10.50–13.00 · Slides 02" --- ::: {.callout-note icon=false} ## What you will do Take a raw NHMS-style extract to an honest logistic-regression baseline the `tidymodels` way: clean the codes, **audit for target leakage**, split with stratification, write a **recipe**, bundle it with a model in a **workflow**, fit, predict, and measure on data the model has never seen. Every later tutorial starts from the objects you build here. **Time:** 50 min live coding + 45 min *Your turn* + 15 min debrief. **How to use this page:** open `tutorials/01_pipeline.qmd` in RStudio (with `ml_um2026.Rproj` open) and run each chunk with the green arrow (or `Ctrl`+`Shift`+`Enter`). Paths like `data/...` assume the project root: set *Tools › Global Options › R Markdown › Evaluate chunks in directory* to **Project** once (see Setup). The rendered page shows the output you should expect. ````` ::: ::: About 12 % have undiagnosed diabetes. Keep that in mind when someone shows you an "accuracy" of 88 %: that is what you get by predicting *No* for everyone. ### Missingness ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} gg_miss_var(nhms_raw, show_pct = TRUE) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](01_pipeline_files/figure-html/missing-1.png){width=960} ::: ```{.r .cell-code} nhms_raw |> mutate(bmi_missing = is.na(bmi)) |> group_by(bmi_missing) |> summarise(n = n(), mean_age = mean(age), pct_rural = mean(residential == 1)) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} `````{=html}
````` ::: ::: BMI is missing more often in older and rural respondents, so it is not missing *completely* at random. Dropping those rows would quietly tilt the model toward younger urban people. We will impute instead — inside the recipe, where it belongs. ### The sentinel problem ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} summary(nhms_raw$sys) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Min. 1st Qu. Median Mean 3rd Qu. Max. -9.0 115.4 125.3 122.7 138.9 184.2 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} ggplot(nhms_raw, aes(sys)) + geom_histogram(binwidth = 2) + labs(title = "Systolic BP, raw", subtitle = "Nobody has a systolic pressure of -9") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](01_pipeline_files/figure-html/sentinel-1.png){width=960} ::: ::: `-9` is the export's code for *not measured*. Leave it in and the imputation step will "impute" nothing, the scaling step will learn a standard deviation inflated by impossible values, and every model downstream will quietly absorb the error. This is the single most common data-cleaning miss in survey-based ML. ## 3 · Clean: sentinels → `NA`, codes → labelled factors ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} nhms <- nhms_raw |> mutate(across(c(sys, dys, rbs, rchol), \(x) na_if(x, -9))) |> mutate( # OUTCOMES: the event level ("Yes") comes FIRST. yardstick treats the first level as the event of interest. undx_dm = factor(undx_dm, levels = c(1, 0), labels = c("Yes", "No")), undx_hpt = factor(undx_hpt, levels = c(1, 0), labels = c("Yes", "No")), undx_chol = factor(undx_chol, levels = c(1, 0), labels = c("Yes", "No")), sex = factor(sex, levels = 1:2, labels = c("Female", "Male")), age_cat = factor(age_cat, levels = 1:5, labels = c("18-29", "30-39", "40-49", "50-59", "60+")), ethnic = factor(ethnic, levels = 1:5, labels = c("Malay", "Chinese", "Indian", "Other Bumiputera", "Others")), residential = factor(residential, levels = 1:2, labels = c("Rural", "Urban")), married = factor(married, levels = 1:3, labels = c("Single", "Married", "Widowed/Divorced")), education = factor(education, levels = 1:4, labels = c("None", "Primary", "Secondary", "Tertiary")), income = factor(income, levels = c(3, 1, 2), labels = c("B40", "M40", "T20")), # odd coding in the source file occupation = factor(occupation, levels = 1:5, labels = c("Government", "Private", "Self-employed", "Homemaker", "Not working")), cons_fv = factor(cons_fv, levels = 1:2, labels = c("Adequate", "Inadequate")), alcohol = factor(alcohol, levels = 1:2, labels = c("Yes", "No")), smoke = factor(smoke, levels = 1:3, labels = c("Current", "Former", "Never")), pa = factor(pa, levels = 1:2, labels = c("Active", "Inactive")), pa_3cat = factor(pa_3cat, levels = 1:3, labels = c("Low", "Moderate", "High")), fam_hx_dm = factor(fam_hx_dm, levels = 1:2, labels = c("Yes", "No")), fam_hx_hpt = factor(fam_hx_hpt, levels = 1:2, labels = c("Yes", "No")), bmi_cat = factor(bmi_cat, levels = 1:3, labels = c("<25", "25-29.9", "30+")) ) levels(nhms$undx_dm) # must be "Yes" "No" - check this every single time ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] "Yes" "No" ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} summary(nhms$sys) # NAs instead of -9s ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Min. 1st Qu. Median Mean 3rd Qu. Max. NA's 82.1 116.9 126.1 129.0 139.9 184.2 228 ``` ::: ::: ::: {.callout-important} ## The event-level rule `yardstick` metrics assume **the first factor level is the event** (`event_level = "first"`). Probability columns are named after the levels (`.pred_Yes`, `.pred_No`); use `.pred_Yes` for ROC, PR and Brier. If your outcome arrives as `0/1`, the default factor order puts `"0"` first and your sensitivity and specificity silently swap. ::: ## 4 · The naive model — a deliberate mistake Throw everything in and see what happens. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} naive_data <- nhms |> select(-id, -undx_hpt, -undx_chol, -pa) # `pa` is an exact recode of pa_3cat; keep one copy set.seed(2026) naive_split <- initial_split(naive_data, prop = 0.80, strata = undx_dm) naive_train <- training(naive_split) naive_test <- testing(naive_split) naive_rec <- recipe(undx_dm ~ ., data = naive_train) |> step_impute_median(all_numeric_predictors()) |> step_impute_mode(all_nominal_predictors()) |> step_dummy(all_nominal_predictors()) |> step_zv(all_predictors()) |> step_normalize(all_numeric_predictors()) lr_spec <- logistic_reg() |> set_engine("glm") |> set_mode("classification") naive_fit <- workflow(naive_rec, lr_spec) |> fit(data = naive_train) naive_preds <- augment(naive_fit, new_data = naive_test) # test data + .pred_class + .pred_Yes + .pred_No roc_auc(naive_preds, truth = undx_dm, .pred_Yes) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} `````{=html}
````` ::: ::: An AUC near 0.98. If a screening model for undiagnosed diabetes ever gives you that, you have not built a brilliant model — you have **leaked the answer**. Which variable is doing it? ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} tidy(naive_fit) |> arrange(desc(abs(statistic))) |> head(8) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} `````{=html}
````` ::: ::: `rbs` — random blood sugar. In NHMS, *undiagnosed diabetes* is **defined** as "no known diagnosis **and** screening blood sugar above threshold". `rbs` sits on both sides of the equation. By the time you have an `rbs` you do not need a model. ::: {.callout-warning} ## Target leakage A predictor leaks when it would not be available — or would not have that value — at the moment the prediction is meant to be made, because it is **caused by, measured with, or defined by** the outcome. | Leak | Looks like | Why | |---|---|---| | `rbs` → undiagnosed DM | AUC 0.98 | the measurement *defines* the outcome | | "on metformin" → diabetes | AUC 0.99 | treatment follows diagnosis | | "days in ICU" → in-hospital death | strong | known only at the end | | patient ID / clinic code | mysteriously useful | encodes site, time or case-mix | | imputing on the full data, *then* splitting | +0.01–0.03 AUC | test rows shaped the imputation | | same patient in train and test | +0.02–0.10 | memorises the person, not the pattern | **Five questions for every predictor:** (1) *When* is it recorded relative to the outcome? (2) Would I *have it* when I want to use the model? (3) Is it part of the outcome's *definition* or confirmation? (4) Does it *change because of* the outcome or its treatment? (5) Does it encode *who/where/when* rather than a fact about the person? ::: ## 5 · The honest predictor set Our use case is a **community screening tool**: things a health volunteer could collect without a blood test or a BP cuff. Out go the four clinical measurements (`rbs` defines this outcome; `sys`/`dys`/`rchol` define the other two and are not available pre-test), the identifier, the other two outcomes, and the duplicate `pa`. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} leaky_vars <- c("rbs", "sys", "dys", "rchol") redundant_vars <- c("pa") # exact recode of pa_3cat -> would make the GLM rank-deficient dm_data <- nhms |> select(-id, -undx_hpt, -undx_chol, -all_of(leaky_vars), -all_of(redundant_vars)) ncol(dm_data) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 33 ``` ::: ::: ## 6 · Split — and lock the test set ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} set.seed(2026) dm_split <- initial_split(dm_data, prop = 0.80, strata = undx_dm) dm_train <- training(dm_split) dm_test <- testing(dm_split) dm_split ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` <3999/1001/5000> ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} dm_train |> count(undx_dm) |> mutate(prop = n / sum(n)) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} `````{=html}
````` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} dm_test |> count(undx_dm) |> mutate(prop = n / sum(n)) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} `````{=html}
````` ::: ::: - `strata = undx_dm` keeps the prevalence identical in both halves. Always do this for outcomes under ~30 %: without it a lucky split gives 9 % in one half and 14 % in the other and your metrics move for no real reason. - `set.seed()` so that you and your co-author get the same split. - **The test set is a one-shot exam.** Every decision from here on — model, hyperparameters, threshold, imputation strategy — is made on resamples of `dm_train`. `dm_test` is touched once, at the end of Tutorial 5. - Time-ordered data? Split by time (`initial_time_split()`). Repeated measures? Split by person (`group_initial_split()`). While we are here, cut the **training** set into five stratified folds. Every honest estimate from now on comes from these (Tutorial 5 explains why): ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} set.seed(2026) dm_folds <- vfold_cv(dm_train, v = 5, strata = undx_dm) dm_folds ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} `````{=html}
````` ::: ::: ## 7 · The recipe: a plan, estimated later ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} dm_rec <- recipe(undx_dm ~ ., data = dm_train) |> step_impute_median(all_numeric_predictors()) |> # numeric NAs -> median of the TRAINING data step_impute_mode(all_nominal_predictors()) |> # factor NAs -> most common level step_dummy(all_nominal_predictors()) |> # factors -> 0/1 indicator columns step_zv(all_predictors()) |> # drop constant columns (dm, hpt, chol are all 0) step_normalize(all_numeric_predictors()) # centre + scale: needed by SVM and NN; harmless for trees dm_rec ``` ::: Nothing has been computed yet. A recipe is a **plan**; `prep()` estimates the plan from the training data (the medians, the levels, the means and SDs) and `bake()` applies it to any data. You will rarely call these yourself — the workflow does — but once, look inside: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} dm_prep <- prep(dm_rec) baked_train <- bake(dm_prep, new_data = NULL) # NULL = the data it was prepped on baked_test <- bake(dm_prep, new_data = dm_test) # the TEST set, transformed with TRAINING medians and SDs dim(dm_train); dim(baked_train) # 33 columns in, ~46 out (dummies), 3 zero-variance gone ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 3999 33 ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 3999 46 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} tidy(dm_prep, number = 1) |> head() # the medians that were learned ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} `````{=html}
````` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} tidy(dm_prep, number = 5) |> filter(terms == "age")# the mean and SD that were learned ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} `````{=html}
````` ::: ::: ::: {.callout-tip} ## Step order matters 1. `step_indicate_na()` — before anything removes the NAs 2. `step_impute_*()` — before dummies (mode on factors) and before scaling (medians in raw units) 3. `step_other()`, `step_novel()` — before `step_dummy()` 4. `step_dummy()` 5. `step_interact()`, `step_ns()` — on the dummy columns 6. `step_zv()` / `step_nzv()` / `step_lincomb()` — after dummies 7. `step_normalize()` — last, so everything the model sees is on one scale 8. `themis::step_smote()` etc. — last of all, training data only (`skip = TRUE` is the default) ::: ## 8 · Workflow = recipe + model ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} lr_wf <- workflow(dm_rec, lr_spec) lr_wf ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` ══ Workflow ════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════ Preprocessor: Recipe Model: logistic_reg() ── Preprocessor ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── 5 Recipe Steps • step_impute_median() • step_impute_mode() • step_dummy() • step_zv() • step_normalize() ── Model ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── Logistic Regression Model Specification (classification) Computational engine: glm ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} lr_fit <- fit(lr_wf, data = dm_train) # preps the recipe on dm_train, bakes it, fits the glm ``` ::: The model you already know, in its familiar form: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} tidy(lr_fit, exponentiate = TRUE) |> # odds ratios per 1 SD (we normalised) filter(term != "(Intercept)") |> arrange(p.value) |> head(12) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} `````{=html}
````` ::: ::: Same GLM as always. tidymodels did not change the maths; it changed the plumbing — and the plumbing is what lets you swap this for a random forest at 2 pm without rewriting anything else. ### Predict on data the model has never seen ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} lr_preds <- augment(lr_fit, new_data = dm_test) lr_preds |> select(undx_dm, .pred_class, .pred_Yes, .pred_No) |> head() ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} `````{=html}
````` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} cls_metrics <- metric_set(roc_auc, pr_auc, brier_class, accuracy, sensitivity, specificity) cls_metrics(lr_preds, truth = undx_dm, estimate = .pred_class, .pred_Yes) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} `````{=html}
````` ::: ::: Read that table slowly: - `roc_auc` around 0.85 — honest, and still useful. - `accuracy` around 0.89 — and `sensitivity` terrible. The default threshold is 0.5 and only 12 % of people are cases, so the model says *No* to almost everyone and is "accurate". Tutorial 6 fixes the threshold. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} lr_preds |> conf_mat(truth = undx_dm, estimate = .pred_class) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Truth Prediction Yes No Yes 36 12 No 80 873 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} lr_preds |> conf_mat(truth = undx_dm, estimate = .pred_class) |> autoplot(type = "heatmap") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](01_pipeline_files/figure-html/confmat-1.png){width=960} ::: ```{.r .cell-code} lr_preds |> roc_curve(truth = undx_dm, .pred_Yes) |> autoplot() ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](01_pipeline_files/figure-html/confmat-2.png){width=960} ::: ::: ## 9 · Swap the engine in one line ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} lasso_spec <- logistic_reg(penalty = 0.01, mixture = 1) |> set_engine("glmnet") lasso_fit <- lr_wf |> update_model(lasso_spec) |> fit(dm_train) augment(lasso_fit, dm_test) |> roc_auc(truth = undx_dm, .pred_Yes) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} `````{=html}
````` ::: ::: Same recipe, same workflow, different algorithm. From Tutorial 2 onwards the line that changes is the model specification: `rand_forest()`, `svm_rbf()`, `boost_tree()`, `mlp()`. ::: {.callout-note} ## From here on: `source("R/prep_nhms.R")` Every later tutorial begins by sourcing `R/prep_nhms.R`, which rebuilds exactly these objects — `nhms`, `dm_data`, `dm_split`, `dm_train`, `dm_test`, `dm_folds` (five stratified folds of the training set), `dm_rec` and `cls_metrics` — so that everyone in the room is working from the same split and the same recipe. ::: ## Your turn (45 min, in pairs) ::: {.callout-tip icon=false} ## Task A · The leakage audit (10 min, no code) For each variable, write **keep / drop** and one reason, from the point of view of a volunteer at a pasar malam with a tape measure and a questionnaire: | Variable | Keep? | Reason | |---|---|---| | `rbs` | | | | `sys`, `dys` | | | | `rchol` | | | | `bmi`, `waist` | | | | `fam_hx_dm` | | | | `id` | | | | `undx_hpt`, `undx_chol` | | | | `dm`, `hpt`, `chol` | | | | `pa` *and* `pa_3cat` | | (hint: `count(nhms, pa, pa_3cat)`) | ::: ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"} ## Solution A `rbs` — drop: it *defines* the outcome. `sys`, `dys`, `rchol` — drop: not available before the test, and they define the other two outcomes. `bmi`, `waist` — keep: a tape measure and scales. `fam_hx_dm` — keep: one question. `id` — drop: an identifier. `undx_hpt`, `undx_chol` — drop: other outcomes measured at the same visit. `dm`, `hpt`, `chol` — all zero by construction (nobody with a known diagnosis is in this sample); `step_zv()` removes them. `pa` vs `pa_3cat` — `count()` shows `pa == "Inactive"` exactly when `pa_3cat == "Low"`: one is a recode of the other. Keep the three-level version; two copies add nothing and make linear models rank-deficient (`recipes::step_lincomb()` would catch this automatically). ::: ::: {.callout-tip icon=false} ## Task B · Two recipes, one model (25 min) Recipe A is `dm_rec`. Recipe B remembers *which* values were missing and uses k-nearest-neighbour imputation. Resample both with the same logistic model on the same five folds and compare. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} rec_b <- recipe(undx_dm ~ ., data = dm_train) |> step_indicate_na(bmi, waist, occupation) |> # B1. why must this come BEFORE imputation? step_zv(all_predictors()) |> # constant columns would confuse the distance below step_impute_knn(all_predictors(), neighbors = ___) |> # B2. try 5 step_dummy(all_nominal_predictors()) |> step_zv(all_predictors()) |> step_normalize(all_numeric_predictors()) rec_b |> prep() |> bake(new_data = NULL) |> glimpse() # B3. which new columns appeared? set.seed(2026) res_a <- fit_resamples(workflow(dm_rec, lr_spec), resamples = ___, metrics = metric_set(roc_auc, brier_class)) set.seed(2026) res_b <- fit_resamples(workflow(___, ___), resamples = ___, metrics = metric_set(roc_auc, brier_class)) bind_rows(median_mode = collect_metrics(res_a), knn_indicator = collect_metrics(res_b), .id = "recipe") |> select(recipe, .metric, mean, std_err) ``` ::: **B4.** Is the difference bigger than the standard error? What does that say about how much imputation strategy matters *here* (7 % missing, MAR)? When would it matter a lot? ::: ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"} ## Solution B ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} rec_b <- recipe(undx_dm ~ ., data = dm_train) |> step_indicate_na(bmi, waist, occupation) |> step_zv(all_predictors()) |> step_impute_knn(all_predictors(), neighbors = 5) |> step_dummy(all_nominal_predictors()) |> step_zv(all_predictors()) |> step_normalize(all_numeric_predictors()) rec_b |> prep() |> bake(new_data = NULL) |> select(starts_with("na_ind")) |> head(3) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} `````{=html}
````` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} set.seed(2026) res_a <- fit_resamples(workflow(dm_rec, lr_spec), resamples = dm_folds, metrics = metric_set(roc_auc, brier_class)) set.seed(2026) res_b <- fit_resamples(workflow(rec_b, lr_spec), resamples = dm_folds, metrics = metric_set(roc_auc, brier_class)) bind_rows(median_mode = collect_metrics(res_a), knn_indicator = collect_metrics(res_b), .id = "recipe") |> select(recipe, .metric, mean, std_err) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} `````{=html}
````` ::: ::: B1: after imputation there is nothing left to indicate. B3: `na_ind_bmi`, `na_ind_waist`, `na_ind_occupation`. B4: the two recipes are within one standard error of each other. With 7 % MAR missingness in predictors of modest importance, the imputation method barely matters. It matters when missingness is heavy, informative (MNAR — e.g. people who skip the weight question *because* of their weight), or sits in your strongest predictor; the missing-indicator is how you let a model *use* informative missingness. ::: ::: {.callout-tip icon=false} ## Task C · Stretch (if you finish early) 1. Collapse any `occupation` level under 5 % into "other" before dummying (`?step_other`). 2. The trees tomorrow will find sex-specific waist cut-offs on their own. Give logistic regression the same chance: add `step_interact(~ starts_with("sex_"):waist)` after `step_dummy()`. Does AUC move? 3. Penalised logistic regression: `logistic_reg(penalty = 0.01, mixture = 1) |> set_engine("glmnet")`. Which coefficients went to exactly zero? (`tidy()` the fitted workflow and filter `estimate == 0`.) ::: ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"} ## Solution C ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} rec_c <- recipe(undx_dm ~ ., data = dm_train) |> step_impute_median(all_numeric_predictors()) |> step_impute_mode(all_nominal_predictors()) |> step_other(occupation, threshold = 0.05) |> step_dummy(all_nominal_predictors()) |> step_interact(~ starts_with("sex_"):waist) |> step_zv(all_predictors()) |> step_normalize(all_numeric_predictors()) set.seed(2026) res_c <- fit_resamples(workflow(rec_c, lr_spec), resamples = dm_folds, metrics = metric_set(roc_auc, brier_class)) collect_metrics(res_c) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} `````{=html}
````` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} lasso_fit <- workflow(dm_rec, logistic_reg(penalty = 0.01, mixture = 1) |> set_engine("glmnet")) |> fit(dm_train) tidy(lasso_fit) |> filter(estimate == 0) |> nrow() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 29 ``` ::: ::: The sex × waist interaction buys a small AUC gain — the simulated truth really does have sex-specific waist cut-offs, and a GLM cannot see them unless someone writes the term down. Tomorrow's trees find it unaided. ::: ## Debrief (12.45) 1. You imputed BMI with the training median. A new patient arrives next year with no BMI. What value is used, and where did it come from? 2. Someone imputes **before** splitting, then splits. Which direction does their test AUC move, and why? 3. `accuracy` for your model is about 0.89. Explain to a clinician in one sentence why that number is meaningless here. ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"} ## Debrief answers 1. The **training** median, stored inside the prepped recipe inside the fitted workflow. It travels with the model — that is what makes a workflow deployable. 2. **Upwards** (optimistic): the test rows' imputed values were computed using test rows, so information crossed the split. Small here; large when missingness is heavy or the imputation model is flexible. 3. "Eighty-eight percent of people do not have it, so a model that says *no* to everyone is 88 % accurate and finds nobody." ::: ## What to remember 1. Clean the codes **before** anything else: `-9` is not a number; `3` is not *Indian* until you say so. 2. Event level first: `levels(outcome)[1] == "Yes"`. 3. Split with `strata`; never look at the test set again until the very end. 4. A recipe is a plan; the workflow preps it on training data only, inside every fold. 5. If the AUC is too good, you leaked. Ask: *could I know this predictor before the outcome?* **Next:** Tutorial 2 — decision trees and random forests (Session 3, 14.00).
